profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-affiliated innovation studio is developing a late-summer pilot workshop inspired by the article on intersections between design thinking and art thinking. This brainstorming meeting brings together the faculty lead shaping the learning experience and the partnerships lead shaping how the concept could travel beyond campus. Their agenda is to generate 3-4 candidate workshop formats, test language that connects art-thinking practices to innovation work without sounding niche or overly academic, and narrow toward one concept to prototype internally as a workshop format. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising workshop directions, a rough structure for the session, and a list of materials or prompts to draft next.

members.name: Dr. Maya Levin
members.expertise: design pedagogy, studio-based learning, reflective practice, curriculum design
members.background: Maya trained in industrial design and later completed a doctorate on creative process in studio education; she now runs interdisciplinary teaching experiments that combine design methods with arts-based inquiry for graduate students and visiting fellows.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to preserve the ambiguity and exploratory depth of studio practice rather than becoming a simplified innovation toolkit, and she is quietly concerned that external-facing programs often strip out the parts of art thinking she sees as most transformative.
hidden_assumptions: A successful pilot mainly tells them whether participants enter a different mode of inquiry, even if the session still feels rough or unresolved.
When people say a workshop needs to be 'practical,' they still include reflective exercises, emotional engagement, and open-ended problem-framing as practical forms of work.
A 'prototype' in this context can be a partially formed artifact, prompt set, annotated collage, or reframed question that makes thinking visible.
Using a 'brief' in an exploratory workshop means treating it as a generative prompt that participants may reinterpret, stretch, or even question.
If a session is called 'evidence from the pilot,' that naturally includes facilitator observations, participant reflections, and signs of deeper reframing rather than only sponsor-ready proof points.

members.name: Jordan Kim
members.expertise: executive education, workshop packaging, corporate innovation programs, stakeholder alignment
members.background: Jordan came from a consulting and innovation-lab background and now translates university research into sponsor-friendly programs, often designing short-format workshops for partner companies and public-sector clients.
members.private_state: He wants a concept that can be packaged quickly as distinctive but legible, and he is quietly wary of anything that sounds too abstract, therapeutic, or difficult to justify when someone asks what the session produced.
hidden_assumptions: A successful pilot mainly tells them whether the format can be positioned credibly and repeated with partner organizations, regardless of whether every pedagogical nuance is perfected yet.
When people say a workshop should be 'practical,' they mean participants leave with tools, framed challenges, and concepts they can bring back to work the next day.
A 'prototype' in this context means a concrete concept, scenario, or low-fidelity intervention sketch that an innovation team would recognize immediately.
A 'brief' is a fixed real-world constraint set that gives the session legitimacy and keeps ideation from drifting.
If a session is called 'evidence from the pilot,' that naturally includes testimonials, visible outputs, and signals that a sponsor could understand as proof of value.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a practical workshop
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both repeatedly say the workshop should feel 'practical' for participants.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means practical in the sense of doing real creative work: sustained reflection, reframing, emotional engagement, and ambiguity-tolerant inquiry that changes how participants approach problems.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means practical in the sense of producing transferable tools, visible outputs, and immediately applicable takeaways for workplace use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-disciplinary workshop planning, 'practical' is an uncontroversial positive term, so each hears confirmation of their own preferred pedagogy rather than a possible divergence.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss wanting the pilot to generate 'good evidence' and show that the concept 'works.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the pilot works if it reveals pedagogical value: participants tolerate ambiguity longer, reframe the prompt in richer ways, and show deeper reflection even if the format still needs refinement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the pilot works if it yields externally legible proof: participants produce recognizable outputs, report clear value, and make the format easier to position with future partners.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both treat 'evidence' and 'what works' as obviously desirable, they never pause to specify what kind of evidence counts; the disagreement is about second-order validation logic rather than the overt plan.

misalignment_points.topic: What a prototype should look like
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that every workshop concept should include some kind of 'prototype' by the end.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the session succeeds if participants externalize emerging insights through artifacts such as annotated collages, reframed briefs, process maps, or unfinished speculative objects that reveal new questions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the session succeeds if participants leave with a recognizable concept prototype such as a service idea, experience storyboard, or testable intervention sketch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to saying 'prototype' in innovation settings, and because prototyping is already expected in design discourse, neither anticipates that their threshold for what qualifies differs so substantially.

misalignment_points.topic: How constrained the brief should be
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the workshop should use a 'brief' so participants have a shared prompt.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the brief can include room for problem-creation, reinterpretation, and even questioning the original framing as part of the art-thinking contribution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the brief defines the task boundary and should keep participants anchored to a stable organizational challenge with clear deliverable expectations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using a brief is standard enough that both see it as a neutral organizing device; the disagreement lies in whether the brief is a starting provocation or a scope container, which feels too implicit to spell out.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this from turning into a thinly branded innovation session with a token creative exercise attached. If we say this sits at the intersection of design thinking and art thinking, the workshop itself has to let people dwell, notice, question, and externalize meaning in a more open studio mode. The pilot does not need to feel finished if it actually changes the way participants inquire.
turns.utterance: I'd love to use this meeting to sketch a pilot that really brings art thinking into innovation practice, not as a decorative layer but as something that shapes the whole experience. If we do it well, the session should feel meaningfully different from a standard ideation workshop.

turns.inner_thought: That's the right positioning challenge. If we can make it feel new without making it hard to explain, there is real potential here for external partners. I need language that sounds distinctive but still practical, so someone outside studio education can immediately see why it matters.
turns.utterance: I think the opening is strong if we can describe it in a way that feels fresh but still practical for people outside the studio world. There's probably a sweet spot where it sounds distinctive without becoming hard to place.

turns.inner_thought: One promising direction is to slow the front end down on purpose: observation, gathering materials, image banks, reflective noticing, staying with uncertainty before making. To me that's practical because it is the real work of changing how people approach a question.
turns.utterance: One format we could test is a workshop that gives the opening phase more weight than usual—more time for observation, collecting materials, building a shared resource bank, and holding off on early closure before teams move into making. I actually think that could still feel very practical if the facilitation is clear.

turns.inner_thought: I can sell a slower opening if it doesn't sound like a long preamble. The session still needs a shape people can recognize, and by the end there should be a prototype people can point to. That helps it feel practical and easier to package later.
turns.utterance: I like that as a differentiator. A longer front end could work well, especially if the whole arc still feels practical and there's a clear sense that participants have created something by the end.

turns.inner_thought: The structure needs a brief, but not one that locks the inquiry too early. The brief should invite interpretation and even some resistance, because that's where art thinking actually enters. I won't say that so bluntly; Jordan will hear 'brief' as structure and that will be enough for now.
turns.utterance: We should probably build it around a brief so everyone starts from a shared prompt. That gives us enough common ground while still letting us see what the format opens up.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, a brief is essential. Ideally it ties to a recognizable organizational challenge so the session has legitimacy and a stable frame. If it's grounded in something real, it will be much easier to talk about with partners and much easier for participants to take seriously.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think a brief will help a lot. If it's tied to a recognizable challenge, that should give the session a strong center and make the whole thing easier for participants to enter.

turns.inner_thought: I want the endpoint to be open enough that a prototype could be an annotated collage, an unfinished object, a reframed question, a visual map—anything that makes thought visible. The danger is that 'prototype' gets narrowed into a neat concept pitch, but I can live with the shared word for now.
turns.utterance: And I do think each group should end with some kind of prototype. It doesn't need to be polished; it just needs to give the session a real endpoint and make the work visible.

turns.inner_thought: Good. As long as prototype means something participants can recognize as an outcome—concept sketch, intervention idea, scenario, something tangible enough to discuss afterward. That will help people feel they made progress and left with something they can use.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Having a prototype at the end will help the workshop land as practical, and it gives people something concrete to refer back to afterward.

turns.inner_thought: For the pilot, I care most about whether participants stay with ambiguity longer, reframe the prompt, and show a different quality of reflection. Facilitator notes, artifacts, and participant reflections all count as good evidence to me. That's what would show the concept works pedagogically.
turns.utterance: For the pilot, I'd want us to think carefully about what counts as good evidence and what would actually show the concept works. I'm interested in making sure we can see what the process is doing, not only how the session looks from the outside.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. We need evidence that travels—participant reactions, visible outputs, and a few examples that make the format legible. If we get good evidence in that sense, we'll be able to say the concept works and move quickly into a partner-facing version.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. If we can be intentional about the good evidence we collect and make sure it helps us show the concept works, the pilot will do double duty for us.

turns.inner_thought: Let's test briefs that naturally reveal whether the workshop can support reinterpretation. Civic belonging and workplace rituals both have enough texture for people to bend, question, and open up. Watching how the brief behaves will tell me a lot about whether the format preserves inquiry.
turns.utterance: Maybe a good next move is to draft two sample briefs and see how the format behaves with each. One could be around civic belonging and another around workplace rituals, since both seem rich enough to test the frame.

turns.inner_thought: That gives us a usable work plan. Keep two concepts in play, map the participant journey, and decide in advance what practical takeaways we want, what kinds of prototype examples we hope to see, and what evidence from the pilot will help us position it. Then I can start seeing the package.
turns.utterance: I like that. Why don't we shortlist two concepts, sketch the participant journey for each, and define the practical takeaways, the prototype examples, and the pilot evidence we want to collect? That should give us a solid basis for an internal test.
